sections.h2: Who values and who collects in Hopkins County?
sections.html:
Hopkins County divides the work between its PVA and its Sheriff. The PVA's staff lists every taxable parcel, measures and photographs buildings, puts a value on each and builds the tax roll that the public may inspect. The office is in the Courthouse Annex, 25 East Center Street, Madisonville, KY 42431, telephone (270) 821-3092.

Billing and collection sit with the Sheriff's Office at 261 Responders Lane, phone 270-821-5661, which serves taxpayers on weekdays between eight and four. Bills still open after April 15 belong to the Hopkins County Clerk, reachable at 270-326-2097.

Bills are written to the name on the parcel as of January 1. A spring buyer may find the old owner still receiving it, and that person should forward it. The Sheriff cannot see new deeds, so a buyer who hears nothing can ring the office or print a copy online.

sections.h2: What does the Hopkins County collection calendar look like?
sections.html:
Mailing normally happens about September 30, and the counter opens October 1. The Sheriff posts four stages through April 15.

Stages of the Hopkins County Sheriff's yearly tax collection (source: Hopkins County Sheriff's Office FAQ)
StageWhat changes
October 1 to November 12 percent discount
November 2 to December 31Face amount
January 1 to January 315 percent added
February 1 to April 1521 percent added

The Sheriff's FAQ prints 21 percent for that final stage. KRS 134.015 itself names only a 10 percent penalty after January, and Revenue's explainer lists a sheriff's add-on fee and commission separately. Call for an exact payoff before paying in February or March.

Sheriff collection stops when business closes on April 15, and whatever is left moves to the Clerk.

sections.h2: Which payment methods does the Hopkins County Sheriff accept?
sections.html:
The office takes online payments and counter payments, and it insists on the whole amount. A partial payment is turned down.

  • Accepted: cash, personal checks, money orders, cashier's checks and cards.
  • An outside processor runs cards and charges 2.5 percent plus 30 cents.
  • Online checks cost $1.50 to process.
  • Write checks to Hopkins County Sheriff.

Escrow does not lift the owner's duty. The Sheriff says the taxpayer must get the bill to the mortgage lender, and a lender cannot pay what it never receives.

sections.h2: How do I estimate and prorate a Hopkins County bill?
sections.html:
The bill math runs as taxable assessment divided by 100, times the rate set for the year. Volunteer fire department fees or watershed taxes, where they apply, are added separately.

The Sheriff's FAQ also gives a sale formula. Divide the last year's bill by 365 for a daily cost, then multiply by the number of days the seller lived in the house. Someone who sells at the end of June would owe 181 days of that daily amount.

Some closing agents wait for the real bill. Compare their number with the Sheriff's method before you sign the settlement statement, and ask which year's bill each of you used.

sections.h2: How do I fight a Hopkins County assessment?
sections.html:
Start with the PVA's office. Under KRS 133.120, a conference with the PVA or a deputy has to come first, ahead of or during the inspection period, and callers can ask to hold it by telephone.

  • The PVA walks through how the number was set and writes up the meeting.
  • If that fails, send the County Clerk a letter or petition no later than one workday after inspection closes.
  • Name the value you think is fair and back it up with land and building descriptions, insurance, cost records, listings, comparable sales or loan papers.
  • Show up for the hearing, personally or through an authorized representative.

The board may reject an appeal if you hold back information it reasonably asks for. Meanwhile, pay on the figure you claimed.

sections.h2: Which Hopkins County owners qualify for a tax reduction?
sections.html:
A homeowner aged 65 or older, or totally disabled, who lives in the property can deduct $49,100 from the assessment for the 2025 and 2026 years.

Applied to the Census middle value of $142,800, that leaves $93,700 to be taxed. The form is completed at the PVA office with proof of age, most often a birth certificate or driver's license. Disability applicants must document benefits received from January through December.

Farmland gets different treatment. The Sheriff's page cites KRS 132.010, which values agricultural land by its production capability, and describes qualifying land as parcels of 10 acres or more used to raise livestock or grow crops, including timber. Nobody can claim more than one exemption on one property within one county and state.

sections.h2: What happens to a Hopkins County tax debt after the Clerk takes over?
sections.html:
Once the Clerk holds the bill, it is a certificate of delinquency, and a lien is entered against the property. A sale of the house does not remove it.

The Clerk's 2025 sale shows the next step. It ran electronically on October 8, 2025, with registration handled at the Clerk's office, 24 Union Street, Madisonville. Buyers paid $5 per priority bill or $10 per current-year bill, capped at $250 in combined fees, and full payment was due by October 10 or the purchase was void.

A buyer of a certificate can load its own fees on the account, so clearing the bill with the Sheriff before the deadline, or with the Clerk afterward, costs less. The Sheriff's website and the Clerk's website do not link, so call the Clerk for current amounts instead of trusting the Sheriff's listing.

sections.h2: How does the local economy shape Hopkins County housing?
sections.html:
Coal and farming built the county's housing stock, and health care and retail now carry much of the load. Madisonville drew its first coal mine in 1869 through an operator for whom Earlington is named, and the Louisville and Nashville Railroad reached the county seat in 1870. Dawson Springs grew in the 1880s as a health resort.

Census figures show a retail-heavy base. Retail sales came to $1.84 billion in 2022, or $41,062 per resident, and health care and social assistance receipts reached about $414 million. Residents spend a mean 21.3 minutes getting to work, and 53.6 percent of people 16 and older are in the labor force.

  • 18,397 households averaged 2.40 people each.
  • Monthly owner costs came to $1,107 with a mortgage and $436 without.
  • Poverty touched 19.3 percent of residents.
  • Builders took out 201 permits in 2025.
  • Persons 65 or older made up 21.0 percent of the population, which matters for homestead claims.

sections.h2: What should a Madisonville-area seller know about Hopkins County?
sections.html:
Hopkins County sits in western Kentucky with Madisonville as seat and largest city. It was created on December 9, 1806 from Henderson County and has 542 square miles of land. The Pond, Tradewater and Green rivers cross it, with flat river valleys in the north and rolling hills in the south and center.

Coal mines work the southern end and farms fill the north, mostly soybeans, corn and tobacco. The Pennyrile Parkway and Western Kentucky Parkway both pass through. Other incorporated places include Dawson Springs, Earlington, Nortonville, Mortons Gap, Hanson, White Plains, Nebo and St. Charles.

  • 45,127 residents in 2025, down 0.6 percent from 2020.
  • A middle owned-home value of $142,800 in the 2020 to 2024 survey.
  • Owners live in 70.7 percent of homes.
  • $56,815 median household income.
  • $837 median gross rent.

Hopkins County Schools covers most of the county, while Dawson Springs runs its own district. Madisonville Community College sits in the county seat, and the Madisonville Messenger is the local daily.

faqs.q: What day does the Hopkins County discount period begin?
faqs.a: Collection opens October 1, after bills go out around September 30. Paying through November 1 earns 2 percent off, and face value applies from November 2 to year end.

faqs.q: Will Hopkins County let me split a bill into pieces?
faqs.a: No. The Sheriff takes the whole amount only and refuses part payments. Cards, cash and checks all work, and cards carry a processor fee.

faqs.q: I closed last month and received no bill. Who do I call?
faqs.a: Call the Sheriff at 270-821-5661. Bills are issued to the January 1 owner and the office does not see new deeds, so a copy can be printed from the Sheriff's website.

faqs.q: Whom do I pay once April 15 has gone by?
faqs.a: Pay the Hopkins County Clerk, phone 270-326-2097 per the Sheriff's page, since open bills go there when April 15 ends.

faqs.q: Do older owners get any relief?
faqs.a: Yes: a $49,100 homestead exemption, filed at the PVA's office on East Center Street. Owners 65 and over who live in the house qualify, as do totally disabled owners.
